extracted.intended_audience: Screenwriters and television writers who work (or seek to work) under the Writers Guild of America (WGA) jurisdiction; WGA members and participating writers
extracted.subtask_description: Plain-language guide to the WGA credits determination process, including eligibility, pre-production and post-production steps, arbitration procedures, and creative/publicity rights for writers on theatrical, television, and new media projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guild authority to determine writing credits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guild has the sole authority to determine writing credits on theatrical, television, and new media projects written under its jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A company cannot guarantee you will receive writing credit; the Guild-developed system is the authoritative process. This pamphlet is not a substitute for the Credits Schedules of the MBA or the Credits Manuals and does not alter their provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company must be signatory to the MBA
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you are dealing with a company that is signatory to the WGA Theatrical and Television Basic Agreement (MBA). Guild Working Rules prohibit members from working for, or selling material to, a company that is not signatory to the MBA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on an agent/manager/attorney; personally call the Guild’s Signatories Department to check status. A company that has applied may not have completed the process. If you work for a non-signatory company, the Guild may not determine credits or you may be ineligible to compete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional writer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for writing credit when selling material to a signatory company, you must be considered a 'professional writer' under the MBA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MBA generally defines 'professional writer' as someone who has received employment totaling 13 weeks as a TV or theatrical writer, or received credit as a writer on a TV or theatrical motion picture (including series), or credit for a professionally produced play or published novel. You may negotiate to be treated as a professional writer even if you don't meet MBA criteria. Guild membership alone does not automatically qualify you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know whether other writers have worked on the project
rubrics_metrics.description: You should know whether other writers have worked on the project before you or are currently working on it; Article 18 of the MBA requires the Company to notify you of any writer assigned to the same project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the Company before agreeing to write or sell material. Use the Guild's 'Article 18 Notice' form to request information. Prior writers (especially on remakes) may affect your eligibility and the likelihood of receiving credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production executive status affects credits
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are employed as a director, producer, story editor, or negotiate producer credit in addition to writing, specific rules for production executives apply and writing credits may be subject to automatic arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production executive status can change the percentage necessary to receive credit in screen arbitrations and triggers automatic arbitration if proposed for credit with non-P.E. writers. Production executives who give only instructions/suggestions may not qualify as writers under the MBA definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover page requirements while writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Until final determination of credits, the cover page of each piece of material must include the name of the first writer followed by the word 'revisions' and then names of subsequent writers; subsequent writers should indicate contributions with 'current revisions by' plus name and date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not remove names of earlier writers even if you believe none of their material remains. The cover page reflects who has worked on the project and does not determine final credits. Contact the Guild’s Credits Department for a sample cover page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep copies and record deliveries
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a credit arbitration, the Arbitration Committee can consider only literary material that was submitted to the company or an authorized representative; writers must keep copies and records of delivery dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach a cover memo/letter with recipient name, date, and description when delivering materials; include this information in cover emails for electronic transfers. Guild registration alone does not prove delivery. Include your filmography with your final draft to aid publicity and residuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing teams: definition and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A team is two writers assigned at about the same time who work together for approximately the same length of time; teams cannot divide joint work into separate individually authored material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MBA does not permit more than two writers to work as a team unless the Guild grants a waiver prior to writing or economic minimums change. If a team member is a production executive, a Guild-approved collaboration agreement and certain forms may be required. Contact the Credits Department early if you question a claimed team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Tentative Writing Credits (NTWC) and Final Shooting Script (FSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of principal photography the Company must send an NTWC and a copy of the FSS to the Guild and each participating writer; the NTWC lists participating writers, proposed writing credits, and source material credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you haven't received an NTWC after principal photography, contact the Guild immediately — delays can interfere with rights and residuals distribution. All participating writers and professional writers who sold material are eligible to compete for credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain current contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the Company and Guild have your current address information to ensure timely delivery of NTWC and FSS and to meet deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If notices are directed to an agent/representative under your contract, ensure they forward notices promptly and update contact info whenever agents change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proper name / pseudonym rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your name appears exactly as it is on file with the Guild; writers must take credit exactly as recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use a nickname/pseudonym you must register it with the Guild; the Guild will not register pseudonyms that don't meet a 'reasonableness' standard and may object later if the pseudonym is not reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement among participating writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating writers may unanimously agree among themselves about which of them shall receive writing credit and the form of that credit, provided it conforms to the MBA and the agreement is reached in advance of arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform the Credits staff member administering an arbitration if you might agree to a particular credit; the Guild can facilitate communication between writers. Unanimous agreement is not available in cases of automatic arbitration or single-writer projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to initiate arbitration (timely protest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's timely protest of the Company’s tentative credits (by the NTWC deadline) typically triggers a Guild arbitration; the protest should be written, state that you are protesting, name the production, and how you believe final credits should read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If credits are subject to automatic arbitration, no protest is necessary. Automatic arbitrations generally cover: (1) production executive proposed for writing credit with other non-P.E. writers, (2) three writers proposed to share screenplay/teleplay credit, (3) 'screen story' or 'television story' credit proposed, (4) 'Adaptation by' credit proposed, and (5) (television) 'Developed by' proposed on certain series. After a timely protest, a Credits Department employee will contact you about procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participating writer investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guild may investigate whether someone is entitled to be listed as a participating writer and therefore eligible to compete for writing credit; entitlement is a contractual interpretation issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guild bears the burden of proving to an arbitrator that an omitted writer is entitled to participating writer status and looks to several factors applied to the case facts. If the Guild finds in favor, it advises the Company to submit a revised NTWC or may submit the matter to legal arbitration if the Company disagrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remake investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: A remake investigation determines whether a film is a remake of an earlier film produced under the Guild’s jurisdiction; if so, credited writers of the original are participating writers on the remake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remake status can make original credited writers eligible to compete for credit on the new picture if the original was under Guild jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and role of expert readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert readers analyze literary material and provide opinions based on their reading; they are drawn from experienced writers familiar with Guild rules and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert readers often have served as arbiters and may be members of the Screen/Television Credits Committee; they will not serve in any other capacity in the same credits determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to request a Pre-Arbitration Hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Pre-Arbitration Hearing may be requested if there's a dispute concerning the materials to be considered in a credit arbitration (e.g., chronological sequence, authenticity, authorship, completeness, identification of materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All issues related to material to be submitted must be resolved before sending to Arbitration Committee; review the Start of Arbitration materials and raise questions promptly. Failure to thoroughly review submitted materials is not a ground to overturn an Arbitration Committee decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Arbitration Hearing process
rubrics_metrics.description: A Special Committee of three Guild members (also TV/Screen Credits Committee members) holds the Pre-Arbitration Hearing; the participant requesting the hearing presents information and other writers meet individually with the Special Committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearings are informal; representatives (attorney/agent) are not required. Pre-Arbitration hearings are usually held quickly due to MBA timeframes; cooperate with the Guild to ensure timely determination. The Arbitration Committee must follow the Special Committee's decisions (e.g., sequence of scripts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision of the Special Committee
rubrics_metrics.description: After receiving all relevant information, the Special Committee considers issues and issues a decision, usually immediately after the hearing, communicated by phone and followed by a letter summarizing reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you disagree with a Special Committee decision you may raise it on appeal to a Policy Review Board after the arbitration decision. The Special Committee's sequencing and rulings bind the arbiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the Credits Manual carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The Credits Manuals contain many specific rules that govern how writing credits are determined and differ by media and circumstances (e.g., screen vs. television, original vs. non-original, production executive status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the Screen Credits Manual and Television Credits Manual before arbitration. If you need copies or have questions, contact the Guild's Credits Department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage thresholds for screenplay credit (screen rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: For theatrical motion pictures the Credits Manual specifies percentage contribution thresholds for screenplay credit depending on whether the screenplay is original or non-original and whether the writer is first/subsequent and a production executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules provided: First Writer – Non Production Executive: >33% (+ 1/2 'Story by' credit) (original) / >33% (non-original). First Writer – Production Executive or P.E. Team: >33% (+ 1/2 'Story by' credit) (original) / >33% (non-original). Subsequent Writer – Non Production Executive: 50% (original) / >33% (non-original). Subsequent Writer – Production Executive or P.E. Team: >50% (original) / >33% (non-original). For television dramatic teleplay credit, percentages don't apply; 'substantially more' to any one of four teleplay elements suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to all deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a deadline for every step in the credits process; the Guild's exclusive authority to determine credits exists for a specified number of days and time is almost always short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No writer can afford to delay learning fundamentals or miss deadlines; missing deadlines can result in loss of rights. The Guild may extend time when possible but overall timeframes under the MBA are strict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify all literary and source material submitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The Company must submit copies of each writer’s literary materials and all source material; participating writers must verify that materials are accurate, complete, dated, and properly sequenced before submission to the Arbitration Committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company is required to submit three copies. If materials are missing, you may be asked to provide copies. Verification must be done before materials go to the Arbitration Committee; you may review materials at the Guild or request they send you copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity / coding of participating writers
rubrics_metrics.description: All credit arbitrations are 'coded'—names of writers are not revealed; writers are referred to as 'Writer A', 'Writer B', etc., according to sequence of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers must abide by coding procedures in statements and avoid revealing identities or information that could identify a writer, company, or production staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements to the Arbitration Committee: content and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating writer may submit a written statement to support a claim to credit. In screen there is no min/max length; the Television Credits Manual suggests statements not exceed three single-spaced pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on contributions as they remain in the FSS—the Arbitration Committee bases decisions on relative contribution to the FSS. Statements must not contain: references to contingent compensation tied to credits; letters/comments of support; irrelevant info that may prejudice a writer; information that reveals any writer's identity; or development-process facts not germane to the arbiter's analysis. Writers generally have 24 hours after notification to prepare a statement (Guild may extend time when possible). Use correct letter codes consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deletions from the Arbiters List
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating writer receives a list of eligible arbiters prior to the arbitration and may delete a reasonable number of names from the list for any reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guild does not inquire about reasons for deletions; primary purpose is to strike potential arbiters for perceived bias or prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration Committee composition and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Arbitration Committee consists of three Guild members; each committee is assigned a consultant. Arbiter names and consultant are confidential; neither the company nor participating writers are told arbiter identities, and arbiters are unknown to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultants answer arbiter questions on rules/policy; confidentiality protects arbiters from retaliation or outside pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of material to the Arbitration Committee (what to submit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participating writer may submit any or all verified literary materials to the Arbitration Committee but may only select from their own materials; generally, submit only drafts necessary for arbiters to assess contributions (last writer often need only submit the FSS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbiters receive verified materials, writers' statements, the credits manual, and a cover memo listing tentative credits, chronological list of materials, relevant rules, and decision deadline. Choose materials strategically—every draft need not be submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision process of the Arbitration Committee and appeal window
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbiters read materials independently, deliberate, and report decisions; if not unanimous, a teleconference is held to try to reach unanimity, though unanimity is not required. The majority decision becomes the Arbitration Committee decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After notification by phone, each participant has 24 hours to request a Policy Review Board (PRB) appeal; strict 24-hour clock is applied. If no PRB is requested within each writer's 24-hour window, the Arbitration Committee’s decision becomes final. Writers may request copies of written opinions without revealing arbiter identities if considering a PRB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy Review Board (PRB) grounds and process
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRB is the appeals stage and can be requested within 24 hours of notice of Arbitration Committee decision; the PRB can only consider whether there has been any serious deviation from Guild policy or procedure in how the arbitration was conducted—not disagreement with arbiter judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRB panel of three Guild members reviews arbiters' written decisions and writers' statements but DOES NOT read/analyze the literary materials submitted to the Arbitration Committee. The PRB may: (1) find no violation and let the Arb. decision stand, (2) send materials back to the original Arbitration Committee for reconsideration with clarification, or (3) direct formation of a new Arbitration Committee to re-determine credits; a second arbitration decision may itself be appealed to a PRB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final credits binding and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the Guild makes a final determination of credits, the Company and participating writers must abide by the Guild’s decision; advertising, publicity, and on-screen credits must comport with the Guild-determined final credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers are not allowed to claim credit contrary to the Guild’s final determination. Report inaccurate or incorrect writing credits immediately to the Guild.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Rights — Viewing the Cut
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating writers on theatrical motion pictures must be given the opportunity to view a cut of the film in sufficient time so approved editing suggestions can be reasonably and effectively implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For long-form television or multi-part closed-end series, the writer must be invited to view the Director’s cut within 48 hours of the company's viewing or be provided a videocassette copy simultaneously if company receives one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Rights — Premieres and sneak previews
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise notified, credited writers on theatrical motion pictures must be invited to the domestic premiere or first domestic festival exhibiting the picture; credited writers on theatrical motion pictures, television pilots, long-form TV, or multi-part series must be invited to the first sneak preview in Los Angeles County.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If required to travel more than 150 miles, the Company must provide first class travel and accommodations. Companies may negotiate better terms in individual agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative Rights — Press junkets and publicity inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless otherwise notified, credited writers on theatrical motion pictures must be invited to domestic press junkets and included in press kits; if required to travel over 150 miles for junket, the Company must provide first class travel and accommodations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If director's identity/background/filmography is included in press materials, the credited writer's identity, background, and filmography must also be included and the writer should be interviewed when the director is, unless otherwise notified. Submit biography/filmography to advertising/publicity at last material submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and reporting inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guild believes certain facts relating to any particular credit determination should remain confidential; writers and representatives should report inaccurate or incorrect writing credits immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the Guild to report errors; confidentiality norms and procedures apply throughout the credits process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time constraints for the entire credits/arbitration process
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire arbitration process—Pre-Arbitration hearing, arbitration, arbiter teleconference, and Policy Review Board—must be completed within the time frames set forth in the MBA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because time is limited, the Guild will, when possible, give additional time to prepare, but participating writers must be mindful of MBA timeframes and cooperate to ensure a timely credit determination.
